To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
minimal-trauma fractures are common in breast cancer survivors; and women who are postmenopausal and those diagnosed with osteoporosis prior are at increased risk of fracture.

minimal-trauma fractures, especially rib fractures, are an important problem for breast cancer (BC)-survivors, especially postmenopausal women and those with a diagnosis of osteopenia/osteoporosis prior to BC.

women who have had a breast cancer diagnosis are at an increased risk of fracture and the likelihood of fracture is increased in women who have a diagnosis of osteopenia or osteoporosis and in those who are post-menopausal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the self-reported frequency of minimal-trauma fractures (MTFs), including rib fractures in women surviving breast cancer.
the frequency and pattern of MTF, and use of bone mineral densitometry (BMD) in women who have survived for at least 3 years after diagnosis with breast cancer.
minimal trauma fracture (MTF), a type of fragility fracture, in a group of women who had survived breast cancer for at least 4 years.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
women who have been treated for breast cancer are at increased risk of MTF and that this risk is greater in those who are postmenopausal.
MTF is a significant problem for BC survivors.
women with breast cancer are at increased risk of fracture, and that risk is increased by pre-existing osteoporotic bone and by post-menopausal status.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the risk of fracture is affected not only by menopausal state, but also by the presence of osteoporosis before the diagnosis of breast cancer, and that the majority of breast cancer survivors have had their BMD assessed.
women with breast cancer should be screened for osteoporosis and treated if appropriate.
women who have breast cancer should have their bone health checked at the time of cancer diagnosis and that this should be repeated at least once every 2 years.
The main takeaway from our work is that
women treated for breast carcinoma should be aware of the increased risk of fracture, especially rib fractures, in their survivorship.
women who are postmenopausal, and particularly those who are postmenopause at the time of breast cancer diagnosis, are at increased risk of MTF.
women treated for breast cancers should be encouraged to maintain a healthy lifestyle and be assessed for osteoporosis and fracture risk.
